## What Claude Code Workflows Are


Claude Code workflows are structured execution patterns that turn a natural-language prompt into a multi-step process: reading files, running tests, editing code, and opening pull requests without you managing each step. A one-shot prompt asks Claude a question and waits for a single response. A workflow gives Claude a goal, a set of tools, and permission to run until the job is done. Between steps, the agent checks outputs, handles errors, and decides what to do next.


For teams shipping real software, the quality ceiling on one-shot prompting is low. You get exactly what you asked for, nothing more. A proper workflow can read your codebase context, run your linter, catch a failing test, and fix it before surfacing a result worth reviewing.


## The Boris Cherny Workflow


[Boris Cherny, who built Claude Code](https://ranjankumar.in/boris-cherny-four-habits-claude-code) , runs five Claude instances in parallel inside his terminal, acting as a fleet commander instead of a coder. The approach rests on three principles:


-


Plan first, then execute: give each agent a written task description before it touches a file.


-


Parallelism by default: isolate tasks so agents run concurrently instead of waiting on each other.


-


Compounding verification: each agent's output feeds the next review cycle so errors surface early.


The bottleneck moves from typing to planning: the limiting factor is whether you can define tasks clearly enough for agents to finish without interruption.


## The Spec Workflow: Plan Before You Build


The fastest Claude Code sessions almost always start with the slowest step: writing a spec before touching any code. When planning and execution happen in the same session, early requirements get buried under hundreds of lines of conversation. Claude loses the signal, output drifts, and you end up correcting things that were settled twenty messages ago. The fix is a hard phase separation: plan in one session, build in another.


Claude Code's[Plan Mode](https://academy.claude.com/courses/ai-native-sdlc-playbook/plan-mode) makes this concrete. Hit Shift+Tab twice and Claude moves into a read-only planning posture, proposing an approach, listing assumptions, and asking clarifying questions without touching a single file. You get a structured plan you can review, edit, and approve before any execution begins, and that spec becomes the source of truth for the next session.


The[Pimzino spec workflow](https://github.com/Pimzino/claude-code-spec-workflow) extends this by automating a four-stage pipeline (Requirements, Design, Tasks, Implementation) where each stage produces a document that seeds the next, giving every subagent working on the same feature the same written brief.


## CLAUDE.md: Institutional Memory for Every Session


Every Claude Code session starts cold with no memory of previous runs.` CLAUDE.md` , checked into git and shared across the team, is how institutional knowledge survives between sessions. See the[Claude Code memory documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) for the full spec on what belongs there. Anthropic's own teams maintain one in each repo, logging mistakes as they surface so Claude stops repeating the same errors.


What belongs in it:


-


Mistake corrections caught in review ("never mock the database layer directly, use the test fixtures in /fixtures")


-


Workflow sequences Claude should follow before committing


-


Safety rails for destructive operations


-


Architecture preferences that aren't obvious from the code itself


Each correction added after a bad output means the next session starts sharper. Over weeks,` CLAUDE.md` encodes the judgment a senior engineer would otherwise re-explain on every review.


## Parallel Sessions with Git Worktrees


[Git worktrees](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree) give each Claude Code session its own isolated checkout so parallel agents never write into the same files at the same time. Spin up a session with the` --worktree` flag (available since Claude Code v2.1.49, February 2026) and Claude creates a separate working tree on its own branch. Four sessions can run against the same repo simultaneously with no merge conflicts mid-run. Worktrees earn their place for tasks scoped to a single feature or unrelated codebase areas. Skip them when work touches shared infrastructure or when one session's output gates the next.

## Slash Commands and Inner Loop Automation


Slash commands are markdown files stored under` .claude/commands/` in your repo. Commit them once and every teammate gets the same automation on clone, with no per-user setup required. A command like` /commit-push-pr` chains three steps that would otherwise require repeated prompting:


-


Stage changes and generate a commit message from the actual diff.


-


Push the branch to remote.


-


Open a[draft PR description](https://willowvoice.com/blog/how-to-write-good-pull-request-description) using the current branch name and spec summary as the description body.


Commands checked into git become executable documentation for how the team expects Claude to behave on routine tasks.


## Verification Loops: How Claude Checks Its Own Work


-


Agent-stop hooks are shell commands that run automatically on task completion. They block Claude from marking work done until your test suite and type checker pass, forcing a retry with the error output as new context.


-


Background verification agents watch for test regressions, type errors, or lint violations while the primary agent implements. Worktrees let the verifier run against a clean branch without blocking the implementer's file state.


-


Browser-based end-to-end testing closes a loop that linters cannot. Encoding it as a slash command means every implementation session ends with a browser verification pass.


## The Multi-Agent Architecture: Orchestrators, Subagents, and Agent Teams


When a task outgrows a single context window, distribute it. An orchestrator agent receives the goal, breaks it into discrete subtasks, and delegates each to a subagent with its own prompt, tools, and model configuration. This pattern suits incident response, large-scale migrations, and adversarial code review well, where parallel branches need to fail independently without stalling the whole job. Run single-agent first. Add orchestration only when context limits or parallelism make the overhead worthwhile.


## Resuming Sessions and Managing Long-Running Workflows


Long-horizon tasks break when sessions time out or context fills. Use` claude --resume` (restart from last checkpoint),` --continue` (reattach without a new context window), or` --teleport` (hand off from local machine to CI runner without losing state) to keep workflows alive across interruptions, including nightly cron-triggered runs. Keep the orchestrator's context lean by having it read result summaries from subagents instead of full execution transcripts.

## FAQs


### What's the fastest way to build a reliable Claude Code workflow without starting from scratch each session?


Populate a` CLAUDE.md` file and check it into your repo. It's where institutional knowledge survives between sessions: mistake corrections, workflow sequences, safety rails, and architecture preferences that can't be inferred from the code itself. Pair it with Plan Mode (Shift+Tab twice) to plan in one session and build in another, so Claude reads a stable brief instead of buried conversation history.


### Boris Cherny claude code workflow vs running a single sequential session: which actually ships faster?


Boris Cherny's fleet model runs five Claude instances in parallel, shifting the bottleneck from waiting on one agent to planning clearly enough that several can run without interruption. The fleet model wins on throughput; sequential sessions win on auditability when you need a committed script to diff against.


### Can you use voice input with Claude Code?


Yes. Claude Code runs in the terminal and IDE, both of which accept text from any system-wide dictation layer. Willow Voice works across all of these surfaces from a single keyboard shortcut, so you can speak a prompt directly into the terminal, a PR description field, or a Linear ticket without switching tools. At ~200ms latency and 98%+ accuracy, dictated prompts land correctly without a correction loop, and codebase auto-tagging means technical terms like variable and function names are recognized from the first session.
